report.currency: Local currency primary (BRL, COP, PEN, MXN, ARS, CLP) with ~USD alongside; tables in millions unless stated
report.verdict: Latin America in 2026 is no longer one growth story. Brazil — the region's largest regulated market at BRL 37bn (~$7.1bn) GGR in 2025 and BRL 20.07bn (~$3.9bn, +15% YoY) in H1-26 — has been switched off by Provisional Measure 1.394/2026 since 6 October, and Lula's re-election on 25 October removes the quickest political route back. The five remaining markets now diverge on maturity rather than size: Colombia (regulated since 2016, 21 online operators, online VAT struck down in April), Peru (cleanest framework, but ISC-on-stakes risk of 1%→5%), Mexico (scale under a 1947 law with a 50% headline IEPS), Argentina (~50% offshore, acquisition-only entry) and Chile (bill still in Congress, framework 2027-28 at best).

summary: **Brazil is dark.** President Lula signed Provisional Measure (MP) 1.394/2026 on 25 Sep 2026 prohibiting the operation, offer, intermediation and advertising of fixed-odds betting (sports and online casino). Deposits stopped on publication, licensed sites and apps went offline on 6 Oct, player balances were refunded via banks 7–14 Oct, and the Ministry of Finance was scheduled to formally revoke all authorisations on 25 Oct (Agência Brasil; Vixio).

**The market that was switched off was the region's largest.** The SPA/MF reported ~BRL 37bn (~$7.1bn) GGR for 2025, the first full year of regulation under Law 14.790/2023, from 79 authorised companies and 25.2m bettors; H1-26 GGR reached BRL 20.07bn (~$3.9bn), +15% on H1-25's BRL 17.4bn (~$3.3bn), averaging BRL 3.3bn (~$0.63bn) a month with 30.8m active registered CPFs (SPA data via BNLData/LAI; brmkt.co reads BRL 20.28bn, 84 licensees, 193 brands).

**Brazil's fiscal stack was material and is now foregone.** Receita Federal collected ~BRL 9.95bn (~$1.9bn) from licensed operators in 2025, including BRL 4.5bn (~$0.87bn) of the 12%-of-GGR legal destinations, plus ~BRL 2.5bn (~$0.48bn) of BRL 30m (~$5.8m) five-year authorisation fees and BRL 95.5m (~$18m) of inspection fees; H1-26 federal tributes were BRL 2.49bn (~$0.48bn). The government's own estimate is BRL 5.3bn (~$1.0bn) less revenue in 2027 (sigma.world citing government analysis).

**Four exit paths, none fast.** Vixio maps (1) permanent ban, (2) sports betting restored/iGaming banned — the position of runner-up Flávio Bolsonaro and the enlarged PL caucus, (3) full restoration if Congress rejects or lets the MP lapse (~4 Mar 2027), and (4) an STF injunction (Justice Fux, petitions from ANJL/IBJR, AGU opposing). Lula's 51.8%–48.2% runoff win on 25 Oct strengthens the executive's hand; a Senate public consultation ran 85.6% in favour of the ban (561,930 votes).

**The region 'changed shape' rather than slowed.** NEXT.io's comparative report (22 Oct 2026, with DATA.BET; 20+ interviews) concludes that 'stage now matters more than size': Colombia is the mature acquirer's market, Peru the cleanest framework with tax unresolved, Mexico scale with entrenched incumbents under a 1947 law, Argentina a provincial patchwork, Chile still pre-regulation.

**Colombia is the structural beneficiary.** Coljuegos' 2022–26 accountability report shows online exploitation rights of COP 396.8bn (~$104m) for Jan–Jul 2026 from 21 authorised operators, 10.8m active accounts and ~1.9m monthly players; the online segment contributed COP 473.0bn (~$124m) for Jan–Aug 2026 and total Coljuegos collections rose 39% YoY, driven by an 84.24% jump in sports betting around the 2026 World Cup.

**Colombia's implied online GGR is approaching the $1bn+ run-rate.** Online rights are levied at 15% of GGR (17% if RTP <83%, Law 1955/2019); 2025 online rights of COP 361.9bn (~$95m) imply ~COP 2.4tn (~$0.64bn) GGR [analyst estimate], and the Jan–Jul 2026 figure implies an annualised ~COP 4.5tn (~$1.2bn) [estimate, World Cup-inflated].

**Colombia's VAT whiplash is the cautionary tale.** A 19% VAT on player deposits under emergency Decree 175/2025 (22 Feb–31 Dec 2025) raised ~COP 1.35tn (~$355m) from the then-14 online operators — roughly 3.7x the sector's exploitation rights. A second emergency (Decrees 1390 and 1474/2025) moved the VAT to a GGR base from Jan 2026, but the Constitutional Court struck the emergency down in April 2026, leaving the VAT inapplicable. Petro's 20 Jul 2026 tax bill sought to make it permanent (COP 1.7tn/~$447m expected from online); its fate under President Abelardo de la Espriella (sworn in Aug 2026) is unresolved [unverified].

**Mexico: scale, but the headline tax is a fiction.** The federal IEPS excise on gaming is 50% on paper (NEXT.io; raised from 30% from 1 Jan 2026 [rate change unverified against the DOF]), yet market experts put the effective rate at ~12–15% after recognised cost-structuring. Entry remains via sub-licensing under incumbents' 1947-law permits; a new regulatory path is 'untested'. No official GGR series exists.

**Argentina: half the market is outside the system.** H2 Gambling Capital (via NEXT.io) puts regulated GGR at ~$1.1bn against ~$1.2bn offshore; advisers with sight of the informal market say up to 80%. The black market is domestic — agents reselling credit over WhatsApp and social media — so site-blocking alone will not fix it. Major provincial tenders (CABA/LOTBA, Buenos Aires/IPLyC, Córdoba) are closed, making acquisition of a licence-holder the only realistic entry route.

**Peru: cleanest framework, tax the swing factor.** Law 31557 (regulated by MINCETUR) went live in 2025; SUNAT levies a 12% tax on the operator's net gaming base plus a 1% ISC on the value of every bet (0.3% Jan–Jun 2025, 1% from 1 Jul 2025 under DS 008-2025-EF). The sector generated PEN 465m (~$134m) in taxes in 2025 (SNJA), of which the ISC yields ~PEN 324m (~$93m) a year. Bill 00519-2026 (filed 6 Oct 2026) would lift the ISC to 5%, targeting PEN 1.62bn (~$467m) — a turnover tax that would consume most of a sportsbook's margin.

**Chile is a cheap option on a 2027–28 framework.** The online gambling bill remains in Congress under the Kast administration (inaugurated Mar 2026); NEXT.io expects legislation to take shape in late 2027 or 2028. Offshore brands already have a foothold; positioning is cheap but its value is wholly contingent on the final tax and licence terms.

**2026 was the year of the ballot box.** Three of the five NEXT.io markets changed governments (Kast in Chile, Mar; Fujimori in Peru, Jul; de la Espriella in Colombia, Aug), and Brazil re-elected Lula on 25 Oct. Legal sources link the election calendar to delayed M&A; dealmaking is expected to return in 2027 with pricing driven by licence transferability, tax exposure and regulatory stability, structured with earn-outs, indemnities and escrow.

**Predictability is worth more than rate.** The NEXT.io taxation chapter's conclusion — 'a predictable 20% is more investable than an unpredictable 12%' — is borne out by Brazil (12%→15% GGR tax, then prohibition), Colombia (19% VAT on, off, on, off) and Peru (ISC 0.3%→1%→5% proposed).

**Enforcement is maturing even where policy is volatile.** Brazil's SPA blocked 25,000+ illegal sites with Anatel in 2025, opened 132 cases against 133 operators, closed 550 bank accounts via 54 financial/payment institutions' reports and removed 324 influencer profiles; ~5m people are blocked (3m Bolsa Família/BPC beneficiaries by STF order; 217k self-exclusion requests in the platform's first 40 days). Colombia's Coljuegos reports stepped-up actions against illegal operators alongside 110,642 authorised slot machines.

**Supply-side gaps are consistent across the region.** NEXT.io flags four: an underdeveloped affiliate sector, fragmented payments, product mixes that miss local demand, and an overlooked retail channel; prediction markets are the wild card. Colombia's retail route is 'genuinely open'.

**Responsible gambling is now the political lever.** Brazil's ban was justified on a Comsefaz estimate of a BRL 62.5bn (~$12bn) household-budget shortfall in 2025 and a Ministry of Health social-cost figure of BRL 38.8bn (~$7.5bn)/yr; Peru's ISC bill is framed as problem-gambling prevention; Colombia already withholds 20% on prizes. Expect advertising, deposit limits and welfare-recipient exclusions to spread.

**Read-through for B2Tech.** Treat Brazil as a 2027 call option, not a 2026 budget line; keep the entity and bet.br assets alive pending the STF/Congress outcome. Colombia is the only market where scale, legal certainty and an open licensing window coincide — enter via concession or acquisition now while VAT is off. Peru is a build case contingent on the ISC vote; Mexico and Argentina are buy-not-build; Chile is a watching brief. Price every market on effective tax and channelisation, not headline rate or population.

segments.name: Brazil — from BRL 37bn regulated market to prohibition
segments.headline: The region's anchor market has been switched off by decree; restoration depends on the STF or a Congress deadline in March 2027, and Lula's re-election makes the executive's position harder to dislodge.
narrative: The regulated fixed-odds market launched on 1 Jan 2025 under Law 14.790/2023 and, by the SPA's own one-year balance (Jan 2026), produced ~BRL 37bn (~$7.1bn) GGR from 79 authorised companies and 25.2m individual bettors (68.3% men; 28.6% aged 31–40, 22.7% each for 18–24 and 25–30). H1-25 GGR was BRL 17.4bn (~$3.3bn) (TCU audit; SPA Panorama Semestral), so the second half accelerated. H1-26 GGR was BRL 20.07bn (~$3.9bn), +15% YoY, or BRL 3.3bn (~$0.63bn) a month, with 30.8m active registrations and semester spend per bettor of BRL 649.60 (~$125) — BRL 108 (~$21) a month, up 5% on H2-25 (SPA data obtained by BNLData under the access-to-information law; brmkt.co's Sigap read is BRL 20.28bn, 84 licensees, 193 brands).

The fiscal stack was heavy but functional: 12% of GGR in legal destinations (BRL 4.5bn/~$0.87bn in 2025), rising gradually to 15% under the late-2025 law change, plus IRPJ, CSLL, PIS/Cofins and payroll contributions for a total federal collection of ~BRL 9.95bn (~$1.9bn) in 2025; BRL 2.5bn (~$0.48bn) of BRL 30m (~$5.8m) five-year authorisation grants; BRL 95.5m (~$18m) of inspection fees; and a 15% income tax on player winnings. H1-26 federal tributes were BRL 2.49bn (~$0.48bn), with sport (BRL 870m/~$167m) and tourism (BRL 678m/~$130m) the largest beneficiaries. Illegal-market estimates ran up to 50% of total play (iGB).

Enforcement had matured: 25,000+ offshore sites blocked with Anatel; 132 administrative cases against 133 operators (80 pending penalties); 54 banks and payment institutions filed 1,255 reports on 1,687 individuals paying unlicensed operators, leading to 550 account closures; 412 influencer cases closed with 324 profiles and 229 posts removed; a centralised self-exclusion platform took 217,000 requests in its first 40 days (37% citing loss of control); and ~5m people are blocked in total, including ~3m Bolsa Família/BPC beneficiaries under the STF's 2024 order.

On 25 Sep 2026 — on the eve of a tight presidential runoff — Lula signed MP 1.394/2026 banning the operation, offer, intermediation and advertising of fixed-odds betting nationwide, calling the sector a 'cancer'. Deposits ceased on publication; bettors could withdraw until 5 Oct; sites and apps went offline on 6 Oct; operators handed balances to banks on 7–8 Oct for refunds on 9–14 Oct, with Caixa as fallback; the Ministry of Finance was to revoke all authorisations on 25 Oct. The government's justification cites Comsefaz's BRL 62.5bn (~$12bn) household-budget shortfall in 2025, the Ministry of Health's BRL 38.8bn (~$7.5bn) annual social-cost estimate, and 20.4% of secondary-school students reporting online betting. Lower-court injunctions (e.g. Stake) were dissolved within 24 hours.

The path back runs through two institutions. Judicially, ANJL and IBJR petitioned the STF on 28 Sep; the AGU asked Justice Fux to keep the ban and await the PGR; Fux deferred until after the 25 Oct runoff, so late October–November is the window for market-wide relief. Legislatively, the MP has drawn 26 amendments, enters urgency status on 9 Nov 2026, could be voted before the December recess or slip to the new legislature in Feb 2027, and lapses around 4 Mar 2027 if not converted — which would restore Law 14.790 and require a follow-up decree on the validity of acts (including revoked licences) during the blackout. Vixio's four scenarios are a permanent ban (least likely given the fiscal hole and club sponsorships worth 6–7% of team budgets per Lula), sports betting restored with iGaming banned (Flávio Bolsonaro's stated position, backed by a larger PL bloc after the 4 Oct legislative vote), full restoration, or judicial resuscitation. Lula's 51.8% runoff win removes the lame-duck scenario and raises the probability that any restoration is partial and conditioned on new restrictions.

Commercially, even a full reversal will not return the pre-ban market: payment rails, sponsorship contracts and affiliate relationships have been severed, the government estimates a BRL 5.3bn (~$1.0bn) revenue loss in 2027, and the black market now has an open field. For an operator, the asset worth preserving is the authorised entity and its compliance record, so that reinstatement — ideally without a second BRL 30m (~$5.8m) fee — can be executed within weeks if the STF or Congress acts. Budget Brazil as a 2027 option with a materially smaller iGaming TAM than 2025.

segments.name: Colombia — the mature benchmark and the region's default beneficiary
segments.headline: Twenty-one licensed online operators, ~COP 4.5tn (~$1.2bn) annualised implied online GGR, a World Cup-driven +39% in regulator collections, and a VAT that the Constitutional Court has (for now) removed.
narrative: Colombia has licensed online gambling since 2016 under Law 643/2001 and Coljuegos' concession model, and its 2022–26 accountability report (Aug 2026) shows the online vertical as the growth engine: exploitation rights of COP 396.8bn (~$104m) for Jan–Jul 2026 from 21 authorised operators, 10.8m active accounts and an average of 1.9m monthly players; by Jan–Aug the online segment had contributed COP 473.0bn (~$124m), with sports betting up 84.24% YoY on the 2026 World Cup and total Coljuegos collections up 39%. Land-based ('localizados') rights rose 12.25% to COP 280.9bn (~$74m) for Jan–Aug across 110,642 authorised slot machines. Total health transfers over 2022–26 were COP 7.21tn (~$1.9bn); the annual Coljuegos series runs COP 990.6bn (~$261m) in 2024, COP 972.2bn (~$256m) in 2025 and a projected COP 1.356tn (~$357m) for 2026.

Online operators pay exploitation rights of 15% of GGR (gross income less prizes), or 17% where the return-to-player is below 83% (Law 1955/2019), and players face a 20% withholding on prizes. Backing out the 15% rate from 2025 online rights of COP 361.9bn (~$95m) implies online GGR of roughly COP 2.4tn (~$0.64bn) [analyst estimate]; the Jan–Jul 2026 figure implies ~COP 2.65tn (~$0.70bn) in seven months, or an annualised ~COP 4.5tn (~$1.2bn) [estimate, flattered by the World Cup]. Fecoljuegos puts the online sector at 0.18% of GDP.

The 2025–26 VAT episode shows how fast the effective rate can move. Emergency Decree 175/2025 applied the general 19% VAT to every player deposit from 22 Feb to 31 Dec 2025 ('the amount available to bet is the deposit less the tax'); the then-14 online operators remitted ~COP 1.35tn (~$355m) — more than COP 123.1bn (~$32m) a month, peaking in Q4 — earmarked for the Catatumbo humanitarian emergency. That is roughly 3.7x the sector's annual exploitation rights, levied on a turnover-adjacent base. A second emergency (Decree 1390/2025, with Decree 1474/2025) re-based the VAT on GGR from January 2026, a concession Fecoljuegos welcomed as recognising 'the real mathematics of the business', but in April 2026 the Constitutional Court declared the emergency decree unconstitutional, rendering Decree 1474 ineffective pending a final ruling. The Petro government's final tax bill of 20 Jul 2026 proposed a permanent 19% VAT on online gambling, expecting COP 1.7tn (~$447m), or 7.8% of a COP 21.8tn (~$5.7bn) package; President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August and the bill's fate is unresolved [unverified].

The licensing window is open and operators keep entering: Coljuegos authorised MrYoker (Global Vitxo S.A.S.) under concession C2261 of 2026 for sports betting, live casino and virtual slots to 2031, taking the count from 14 at end-2025 to 21 by July 2026. NEXT.io characterises Colombia as the market that 'rewards acquisition' and notes the retail route is 'genuinely open' — relevant given Coljuegos' large localizado estate and Colombia's cash-heavy payments culture.

For B2Tech, Colombia is the only Latin American market where legal certainty, scale and an available licence coincide in 2026. The risks are fiscal rather than regulatory: a right-leaning administration may be less inclined to re-impose the VAT, but the Constitutional Court's final word is pending and a 19%-on-GGR VAT stacked on 15% rights would take the effective GGR tax to ~34% before prize withholding. Model both states.

segments.name: Mexico — scale under a 1947 law, with a 50% excise that nobody pays in full
segments.headline: The largest of the five NEXT.io markets by scale, but entry runs through incumbents' permits and the tax case depends on structuring the regulator tolerates.
narrative: Mexico's gambling framework is the Ley Federal de Juegos y Sorteos of 1947, administered by SEGOB's Dirección General de Juegos y Sorteos via a 2004 regulation (tightened in 2023 to curb new slot permits [unverified detail]). There is no published official GGR series; NEXT.io's report describes Mexico as 'now the largest market in this report' with 'entrenched incumbents', and H2-type estimates were not available to verify. Treat any market-size figure as [unverified].

Taxation is the key distortion. The federal IEPS excise on games with wagers is 50% on paper (NEXT.io), up from the long-standing 30% as part of the 2026 federal revenue package [rate change not verified against the Diario Oficial]; the base is receipts net of prizes paid, i.e. GGR-like [base per LIEPS art. 18, unverified], and states layer their own levies [unverified]. Market experts interviewed by NEXT.io put the effective rate at roughly 12–15% after 'recognised cost-structuring'. That gap is the investment thesis and the risk in one line: profitability depends on structures that a future administration or SAT audit could reject.

Licensing is closed in practice. New federal permits have not been issued for years; the route to market is a sub-licence under an existing permit-holder (Caliente, Codere, Logrand, Big Bola and others are the commonly cited incumbents [unverified list]). NEXT.io notes a new regulatory path that 'remains untested but could replace sub-licensing as the only route to market'. Until it is tested, assume incumbents control access, pricing and timing.

Operationally, Mexico combines the region's deepest retail casino estate with fast-growing mobile sportsbook, and co-hosted the 2026 World Cup. Payments are card- and OXXO/cash-voucher-heavy with SPEI transfers; the report flags payments fragmentation and an immature affiliate market as supplier gaps. For B2Tech this is a buy-or-partner market: a sub-licence with a strong incumbent (with explicit tax-structure warranties) or a minority stake in a local operator, not a greenfield build.

segments.name: Argentina — provincial patchwork and the channelisation test
segments.headline: About $1.1bn of regulated GGR against ~$1.2bn offshore; tenders are closed and the black market is domestic and social-media-based, so entry means buying a licence-holder.
narrative: Online gambling in Argentina is regulated province by province: the City of Buenos Aires (LOTBA), Buenos Aires Province (IPLyC), Córdoba, Mendoza, Santa Fe, Entre Ríos and others each run their own licensing, tax and technical regimes, and there is no national regulator or consolidated statistics. H2 Gambling Capital figures cited in the NEXT.io report put the regulated market at about $1.1bn in GGR against roughly $1.2bn offshore — a ~48% channelisation rate — while advisers with sight of the informal market estimate the unlicensed share at up to 80%.

The informal market's shape is the policy problem. It is largely domestic, run by agents who resell gambling credit through social media and messaging apps — in one executive's words, 'the bookmaker model of 40 years ago, moved onto WhatsApp'. DNS blocking and payment-blocking, the tools that work against offshore sites, are blunt instruments against a cash-and-Mercado-Pago agent network, which is why NEXT.io frames channelisation as 'the test regulation has not yet passed'.

Taxation combines provincial GGR-based levies (rates differ by jurisdiction) with a national indirect tax on online bets introduced in 2021 at a base rate on stakes, with higher rates for foreign or non-cooperating-jurisdiction operators [rates unverified]. Combined with inflation, FX controls and periodic restrictions on card use for gambling, the effective burden is hard to model and differs materially between CABA and PBA.

The main tenders are closed, so NEXT.io concludes that acquisition of a licence-holder is the only realistic route to entry; deal activity has been slowed by the political calendar but is expected to return in 2027, with buyers pricing licence transferability (which requires provincial consent) and tax exposure, and protecting themselves with earn-outs, escrow and indemnities. For B2Tech, Argentina is a platform-and-content opportunity through existing licensees (Codere, bplay/Boldt, Betsson, bet365 partners and local lottery operators are among those active [list unverified]) rather than a direct-licence play.

segments.name: Peru — the cleanest framework, with a turnover tax as the swing factor
segments.headline: Law 31557 gave Peru a workable MINCETUR licensing regime and a 12% GGR-type tax; the 1% ISC on every bet is the unresolved dispute, and Bill 00519-2026 would raise it to 5%.
narrative: Peru's remote gaming and sports betting market operates under Law 31557 (2022), regulated by MINCETUR, with licensed platforms live since 2025; MINCETUR said in January 2025 that more than 60 companies had been authorised to exploit remote-gaming/sports-betting platforms, and a secondary reading of the MINCETUR register on 1 Oct 2026 lists 46 remote-gaming authorisations [secondary]. NEXT.io rates the regime 'among the most workable anywhere' — operators praise the clarity of the authorisation process, the technical standards and the absence of local-ownership requirements.

SUNAT administers two taxes on authorised platforms: the Impuesto a los Juegos a Distancia y Apuestas Deportivas a Distancia at 12% of the taxable base (Law 31557 art. 42), and the Impuesto Selectivo al Consumo (ISC), introduced by Legislative Decree 1644 (Sep 2024), levied on 'the value of each bet' including bonuses — 0.3% from Jan to 30 Jun 2025 and 1% from 1 Jul 2025 under DS 008-2025-EF. The Sociedad Nacional de Juegos de Azar reports the activity generated PEN 465m (~$134m) in fiscal revenue in 2025; the ISC alone yields about PEN 324m (~$93m) a year at 1%, which implies annual stakes of roughly PEN 32bn (~$9.3bn) and a 12%-tax base of ~PEN 1.2bn (~$0.34bn) [analyst estimate; assumes 465m covers only these two taxes].

The dispute is twofold. First, Congress had approved a bill correcting how the ISC applies to domestic versus foreign platforms (and criminalising match-fixing); the Executive observed it in July 2025, it was archived in June 2026 before the new legislature, and the Chamber of Deputies revived it in September 2026 as proposal 00389/2026-2031-CD. Second, on 6 Oct 2026 deputy Luis Masco Cáceres (Partido Cívico Obras) filed Bill 00519-2026 to raise the ISC from 1% to 5% of each bet, keeping the base, with an exposición de motivos projecting collections of ~PEN 1.62bn (~$467m) and framing the measure as problem-gambling prevention. A 5% turnover tax equals roughly half of a typical sportsbook's gross margin and would push effective GGR-equivalent taxation above 60% for sports [analyst calc], making channelisation collapse the likely outcome.

Politically, Keiko Fujimori took office in July 2026 after interim president José María Balcázar; the new Congress (bicameral from 2026) has shown both pro-enforcement and pro-tax instincts, with the Executive pursuing clandestine operators while the ISC debate runs. For B2Tech, Peru is the one greenfield build case among the five, but the go/no-go hinges on the ISC vote: at 1% the market is investable; at 5% it is not.

segments.name: Chile — the pre-regulation option
segments.headline: The last major Latin American market without online regulation; a bill sits in Congress under the Kast government and NEXT.io expects a framework only in late 2027 or 2028.
narrative: Chile's Superintendencia de Casinos de Juego (SCJ) regulates land-based casinos, while Polla Chilena and Lotería de Concepción hold state lottery and sports-pool rights; online betting has no licensing regime and is served by offshore brands, several of which sponsor Chilean football and have been the target of SCJ complaints and blocking litigation [details unverified]. The online gambling bill passed the Chamber of Deputies and has been in the Senate for an extended period; NEXT.io reports that under President José Antonio Kast (inaugurated March 2026) legislation is 'expected to take shape in late 2027 or 2028'.

The bill's parameters as last reported — a GGR-based tax, a fixed-term licence, a responsible-gambling levy and a transition period requiring offshore operators to exit before applying [all unverified pending the final text] — will determine whether early positioning is worth anything. NEXT.io frames Chile as 'an option': positioning is cheap today, but its value depends entirely on the framework that eventually arrives, and the regulator's stance toward operators that served the grey market pre-regulation is the key unknown.

No official online market figure exists; estimates circulate in the low hundreds of millions of US dollars [unverified]. Chile's high card penetration, strong banking rails and comparatively high GDP per capita make it attractive once regulated, but a Kast-era bill could carry tighter advertising and product rules than the 2023 Chamber text.

For B2Tech the rational posture is a watching brief with a local counsel retained: no capital deployment until the Senate text fixes tax, licence fees and grey-market treatment, but readiness to file in the first window.

segments.name: Cross-market: tax, licensing, payments, responsible gambling and advertising
segments.headline: The headline rate is the least reliable input; what matters is the base (turnover vs GGR), the stack (VAT, prize withholding, excise), and the likelihood the rule survives the next election.
narrative: On tax base, the region splits three ways. GGR-based regimes: Brazil (12% rising to 15%, plus corporate taxes and 15% on winnings), Colombia (15%/17% exploitation rights plus 20% on prizes), Peru's core tax (12%). Turnover-adjacent add-ons: Peru's ISC on every bet (1%, 5% proposed), Colombia's 2025 VAT on deposits (19%), Argentina's national indirect tax on stakes. Headline-vs-effective regimes: Mexico's 50% IEPS versus a ~12–15% effective rate. NEXT.io's taxation chapter concludes that the headline rate a government announces is the least reliable part of any Latin American investment case; 'a predictable 20% is more investable than an unpredictable 12%'.

On licensing, availability is the differentiator. Colombia issues concessions continuously (14 → 21 online operators in seven months; terms to 2031); Peru's MINCETUR authorisation is open and praised for clarity; Brazil's BRL 30m (~$5.8m) five-year authorisation was open but is now revoked; Mexico's federal permits are closed, leaving sub-licensing; Argentina's provincial tenders are closed, leaving acquisition; Chile has no licence to apply for. Local-ownership rules are not a barrier in Colombia or Peru; Brazil required a Brazilian-incorporated entity with a local partner holding at least 20% [recall; unverified].

Payments remain fragmented, per NEXT.io's supplier-gap analysis. Brazil was Pix-dominant (instant, free, bank-linked) and the blackout required banks to refund balances by CPF — showing how tightly rails and regulation are coupled; Colombia relies on PSE bank transfers, Nequi/Daviplata wallets and cash via Efecty/Baloto, with the 2025 VAT having been charged at the deposit; Mexico on cards, SPEI and OXXO cash vouchers; Argentina on Mercado Pago and cards under FX controls, with the unlicensed market running on agent cash; Peru on Yape/Plin wallets and cards; Chile on cards and bank transfers [country payment mixes are analyst characterisations, not regulator statistics].

Responsible-gambling and advertising rules are tightening everywhere and are now the political justification for fiscal measures. Brazil had the most developed toolkit before the ban — central self-exclusion (217k requests in 40 days), welfare-recipient blocking (~3m), influencer takedowns (324 profiles), payment-institution reporting (1,255 reports, 550 closures) — and then prohibited advertising and sponsorship outright. Peru's ISC bill is explicitly framed as problem-gambling prevention. Colombia's regulator pairs growth with responsible-gambling campaigns and prize withholding. Expect deposit-limit mandates, ad windows and sponsorship curbs to spread to Colombia and Peru within 12–24 months.

For an operator, the practical hierarchy for 2027 planning is: (1) Colombia — enter or scale now; (2) Peru — build, conditional on the ISC vote; (3) Brazil — preserve optionality for a smaller, sports-weighted market; (4) Mexico and Argentina — partner or acquire with tax and licence-transfer protections; (5) Chile — monitor.

highlights.text: Colombia's licensing window is open and growing: 14 → 21 online operators between end-2025 and July 2026, concessions running to 2031, 10.8m active accounts, and regulator collections +39% YoY (sports betting +84% on the World Cup). Implied annualised online GGR ~COP 4.5tn (~$1.2bn) [estimate].

Colombia's 19% online VAT is currently void after the Constitutional Court struck down the emergency decree in April 2026, leaving the effective GGR tax at 15% (17% for low-RTP products) — the lowest certain rate among the regulated markets.

Peru's MINCETUR regime is rated among the most workable anywhere: open authorisation, clear technical standards, 12% GGR-type tax, no local-ownership barrier — a genuine greenfield build case if the ISC stays at 1%.

Brazil's authorised-entity status is a valuable option: Vixio's scenarios include STF injunctive relief or MP lapse by ~4 Mar 2027 with a follow-up decree reinstating compliant operators without a second BRL 30m (~$5.8m) fee. A sports-only restoration is the modal outcome.

M&A is delayed, not cancelled: NEXT.io's sources expect deal flow to return in 2027 with valuations driven by regulatory certainty, favouring buyers who can underwrite licence transferability and tax exposure with earn-outs and escrow — a window for a disciplined acquirer in Argentina and Mexico.

Supply-side gaps recur across all five markets — underdeveloped affiliates, fragmented payments, mismatched product mixes and an overlooked retail channel — giving a B2B/B2C hybrid like B2Tech room to differentiate on localisation rather than price.
Chile offers cheap optionality: offshore brands already have a foothold, and early relationships with local counsel, media and football properties can be secured ahead of a 2027–28 framework.

lowlights.text: Brazil demonstrates the ultimate regulatory tail risk: a BRL 37bn (~$7.1bn) regulated market, 84 licensees and BRL 2.5bn (~$0.48bn) of paid licence fees were eliminated by a single provisional measure, and Lula's 25 Oct re-election removes the lame-duck path to reversal.

Even a Brazilian reversal returns a smaller market: payment rails, sponsorships and affiliates are severed, the government books a BRL 5.3bn (~$1.0bn) 2027 revenue loss, and the politically viable compromise bans iGaming — the higher-margin vertical.

Peru's ISC on stakes could go from 1% to 5% (Bill 00519-2026, filed 6 Oct 2026, targeting PEN 1.62bn/~$467m): a 5% turnover tax would exceed half of typical sportsbook gross margin and make the regulated market uncompetitive against offshore.

Colombia's VAT could return: the Constitutional Court's final ruling on Decree 1474/2025 is pending and the July 2026 bill to make the 19% VAT permanent (COP 1.7tn/~$447m expected) is in the new Congress; a GGR-based VAT stacked on 15% rights would lift effective GGR tax to ~34%.

Mexico's profitability rests on cost-structuring that converts a 50% headline IEPS into a ~12–15% effective rate; a tax-authority challenge or political shift would re-price every incumbent and sub-licensee at once, and the 1947 law offers no modern licensing route.

Argentina's black market is domestic and agent-based (WhatsApp credit resale), with regulated GGR ~$1.1bn vs ~$1.2bn offshore and adviser estimates of up to 80% unlicensed; licences are closed, so entry means paying for a provincial licence-holder whose transferability needs regulator consent.

Data quality is uneven: only Brazil (pre-ban) and Colombia publish regulator-grade GGR or proxy series; Mexico, Argentina, Peru and Chile require reliance on H2/trade estimates or back-solving from tax receipts, which widens valuation error bars.

forecast.intro: The regional bridge from 2025 to 2027 is dominated by Brazil: the ~BRL 40bn (~$7.7bn) annualised regulated GGR run-rate of H1-26 goes to zero from Q4-26 and, in our base case, returns in H2-27 as a sports-only market worth perhaps 40–55% of its prior size [analyst estimate]. Against that, Colombia adds growth (implied online GGR ~COP 4.5tn/~$1.2bn annualised, World Cup-inflated, with VAT void), Peru's trajectory bifurcates on the ISC vote, Mexico and Argentina move only through M&A, and Chile contributes nothing before 2028. Three new presidents (Chile, Peru, Colombia) and a re-elected Lula set the policy tone; NEXT.io's sources expect much of what stalled in 2026 to resolve within 12 months.

forecast.view: **Brazil:** we assign roughly 55% probability to a sports-betting-only restoration via amended MP or follow-on bill by mid-2027, 25% to full restoration (STF injunction or MP lapse with reinstatement decree), 20% to prohibition persisting through 2027 [analyst judgement]. Any restored regime will carry tighter advertising, deposit limits and likely the 15% GGR rate from day one; licence fees are unlikely to be re-charged for compliant operators. **Colombia:** online GGR growth of 20–30% in 2027 [est.] off a World Cup-inflated 2026 base, with the main swing being the VAT — we think a right-leaning government and the Constitutional Court make a permanent 19% VAT less likely than not, but a GGR-based version at a lower rate is a plausible compromise. **Peru:** the 5% ISC is unlikely to pass unamended, but a 2–3% rate is a realistic risk; the ISC-correction bill for foreign platforms is likelier to pass. **Mexico:** no structural change before the 2027 mid-terms; effective tax stays well below the 50% headline unless SAT acts. **Argentina:** provincial regulators will prioritise agent-network enforcement and payment controls over new licensing; expect two or three licence-holder transactions in 2027. **Chile:** Senate passage in 2027 is possible; licences no earlier than 2028. **Leverage direction:** regional regulated GGR falls in 2027 versus 2026 because of Brazil, even as the other five grow; operators with Brazil concentration face covenant pressure, which will surface distressed assets.
